prompt: Without `@Override`, the `Book` class with `tostring()` compiles. What does the annotation add?

choices.text: It makes `tostring` count as `toString`
choices.why: No annotation changes which method overrides which; the spelling decides.

choices.text: A check: refuse if nothing above is overridden
choices.why: Right: `method does not override or implement a method from a supertype`.

choices.text: Faster calls, because the JVM can skip the lookup
choices.why: `@Override` has SOURCE retention; the JVM never sees it.

prompt: `lendBook` carries `@Deprecated(since = "2.0", forRemoval = true)`. What happens when `Counter` calls it?

choices.text: `javac` refuses to compile `Counter`
choices.why: It compiled with one warning; nothing about deprecation is an error.

choices.text: It compiles, and the call throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when it runs
choices.why: `java Counter` printed `lent 978-0-13-468599-1`: a deprecated method works as before.

choices.text: A `[removal]` warning at the call, and it runs as before
choices.why: Right: the warning is about a future version, not this one.

choices.text: Nothing, unless `-Xlint:deprecation` is given
choices.why: That is the plain `@Deprecated`; `forRemoval` warns by default.

prompt: Match each annotation to what the compiler does with it.

pairs.right: refuses a method that overrides nothing
notes or warns at every use
stays quiet about a named kind of warning
refuses an interface with two abstract methods

prompt: Where should `@SuppressWarnings("removal")` go?
hint: Think of the next warning nobody has seen.

choices.text: On the class, so one annotation covers every method in it
choices.why: That also hides every later removal warning in the class, including ones nobody has read.

choices.text: On the deprecated method itself, in the library
choices.why: The library's author wants callers warned; silencing belongs to a caller that decided.

choices.text: On the smallest declaration that needs it, such as one method
choices.why: Right: a method rather than a class, with a comment when the reason is not obvious.

prompt: Why did `javac` refuse `Rule`?

choices.text: It has two abstract methods, and the annotation promises one
choices.why: Right: `@FunctionalInterface` promises exactly one, so a lambda can implement it.

choices.text: An interface may not carry any annotation
choices.why: Interfaces carry annotations all the time; this one broke the promise it made.

choices.text: `describe` returns a `String`, and functional interfaces return only `boolean`
choices.why: The return type is free; the count of abstract methods is what matters.

prompt: Three annotations were placed on `Target`. How many did `getAnnotations()` return while the program ran?
hint: Only one retention reaches the JVM.

choices.text: Three, all of them
choices.why: `InSource` and `InClassFile` never reached the running program.

choices.text: Two: the ones written into the class file
choices.why: Two were in the class file, and only the `RUNTIME` one was loaded.

choices.text: One, `@AtRunTime`
choices.why: Right: the only one with `RUNTIME` retention.

choices.text: None, because nested annotation types are invisible to reflection
choices.why: It printed `@Kept.AtRunTime()`; nesting changes nothing.

prompt: Order the retentions from the one that lives shortest to the one that lives longest.
`javap -v` listed `Kept$InClassFile` under `RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations`. What does that mean?

choices.text: The annotation was dropped by the compiler
choices.why: Dropped annotations are listed nowhere; `InSource` is the one that was dropped.

choices.text: It is in the class file, and the JVM does not load it
choices.why: Right: `CLASS` retention, there for bytecode tools and invisible to reflection.

choices.text: The JVM loads it but only `javap` is allowed to read it
choices.why: Nothing loads it at run time; `javap` reads the file, not a running JVM.

choices.text: It is hidden from reflection only until `setAccessible(true)` is called
choices.why: `setAccessible` is about private members; it cannot bring back what was never loaded.

prompt: You write a test framework's `@Test` annotation and forget `@Retention`. Every test is then ignored. Why?
hint: What is the default retention, and who reads the annotation?

choices.text: Without `@Retention` the annotation does not compile
choices.why: It compiles; the default is simply not the one a framework needs.

choices.text: The default is `CLASS`, so reflection finds no `@Test` on any method
choices.why: Right: `isAnnotationPresent` answers false, and the runner skips every method as it skipped `helper`.

choices.text: The default is `SOURCE`, and the compiler rejects methods marked with it
choices.why: The default is `CLASS`, and nothing is rejected: the methods compile and are never found.

prompt: `Runner` printed `FAILED: acceptsTheSecondBook`. What was actually wrong?

choices.text: `validIsbn` has a bug in its weights
choices.why: It accepted `978-0-13-468599-1` and rejected the typo, so the weights work.

choices.text: Reflection called the method on the wrong object
choices.why: There was one instance, and the other two checks ran on it correctly.

choices.text: `getDeclaredMethods` ran it before the class was ready
choices.why: Order does not matter here; every check is independent.

choices.text: `978-1-61729-136-8` has a wrong check digit
choices.why: Right: it was invented for earlier examples and nobody computed it; the check found real bad data.

prompt: A method called with `m.invoke(instance)` throws `AssertionError`. What does `Runner` catch, and where is the `AssertionError`?

choices.text: An `InvocationTargetException`, with the `AssertionError` as its cause
choices.why: Right: so `Runner` reports `e.getCause().getMessage()`.

choices.text: The `AssertionError` itself, thrown straight through `invoke`
choices.why: Reflection wraps whatever the method throws; catching `AssertionError` would miss it.

choices.text: An `IllegalAccessException`, because the check failed
choices.why: That is for calling something you may not access; a failing check is a different thing.

prompt: The part of the library that lets a running program list a class's methods and call them by name is called ___.
What does `@Target(ElementType.FIELD)` on `@NotBlank` decide?

choices.text: Which object the validator checks
choices.why: The validator checks whatever it is given; `@Target` is about where the annotation is written.

choices.text: That it may be written only on fields
choices.why: Right: on a method it is refused at compile time.

choices.text: That the field it marks must be `private`
choices.why: `name` and `email` are package-private and were marked fine.

choices.text: That reflection can read it while the program runs
choices.why: That is `@Retention(RUNTIME)`, the other annotation on it.

prompt: The second `Member` had `phone` set to `""`. Why is it not in the list of problems?
hint: What does the validator do with a field that has no `@NotBlank`?

choices.text: An empty string is not blank
choices.why: `"".isBlank()` is true; the field was never checked.

choices.text: `phone` has no `@NotBlank`, so `getAnnotation` returned `null` and it was skipped
choices.why: Right: the rule lives on the field, and no rule means no check.

choices.text: `getDeclaredFields` skips fields declared after the annotated ones
choices.why: It returns every field the class declares.

prompt: An annotation type is declared with the keyword `___`, and an element such as `message()` gets a value used when none is written with `default`.
hint: An at-sign and a familiar keyword.

prompt: A colleague adds `@NotBlank` to a field of a new class and is surprised that blank values still get saved. The annotation is declared exactly as in this lesson. What is the most likely reason?
hint: An annotation does nothing by itself.

choices.text: The new class is in another package, so the annotation is invisible
choices.why: Visibility of the annotation type is a compile-time matter, and it compiled.

choices.text: `RUNTIME` retention is lost when the object is saved
choices.why: Retention is about the class, not about objects or saving them.

choices.text: Nothing in the program calls the validator on that class's objects at all
choices.why: Right: a field marked with an annotation no code reads is a field with a comment on it.

prompt: Which of these may be the type of an annotation element like `message()`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The value has to be written into the class file.

choices.text: `String`
choices.why: Yes: `message()` is one.

choices.text: `int[]`
choices.why: Yes: primitives and arrays of them are allowed.

choices.text: `java.util.List<String>`
choices.why: No: a collection cannot be written into a class file as a constant; an array can.

choices.text: `Member`
choices.why: No: an ordinary class is not among the allowed types.

prompt: Which annotation would make `Kept` print two lines instead of one, with no other change?
hint: Which of the other two could reach the running program?

choices.text: Adding `@Target(ElementType.TYPE)` to `InClassFile`
choices.why: `@Target` decides where it may be written, not how long it lives.

choices.text: Changing `InClassFile`'s retention to `RUNTIME`
choices.why: Right: then the JVM loads it and `getAnnotations()` returns both.

choices.text: Adding `@Override` to `main`
choices.why: That is a compile-time check, and `main` overrides nothing, so it would not even compile.

choices.text: Calling `setAccessible(true)` on `Target.class` before asking
choices.why: `setAccessible` is about access to members; it cannot load an annotation the JVM never kept.

prompt: A framework method has `@GetMapping("/books")` on it. Which retention must `@GetMapping` have for the framework to route requests by it?
hint: The framework reads it while the program runs.

choices.text: `SOURCE`
choices.why: Gone after compiling; nothing would be left to route by.

choices.text: `CLASS`
choices.why: In the class file but never loaded, so reflection would not see it.

choices.text: `RUNTIME`
choices.why: Right: every annotation a framework reads at run time has it.
